title: Arabic grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is Modern Standard Arabic, fully vowelled, with a reading in Latin letters.

units.title: Numbers, time and more than one

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Arabic conversation.

goal.t: مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا سَارَةُ. أَنَا مِنْ كَنَدَا.
goal.r: marḥaban, anā sāratu. anā min kanadā.
goal.tr: Hello, I'm Sarah. I'm from Canada.

blocks.p: Look at what is missing in this conversation: Arabic has no word for “am”, “is” or “are” in the present. {{أَنَا سَارَةُ}} is, word for word, “I Sarah”. You simply put the two side by side.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Egypt.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{أَنَا|anā}} is “I”, for a man or a woman. “You” depends on who you're talking to: {{أَنْتَ|anta}} to a man, {{أَنْتِ|anti}} to a woman. Karim says {{مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟}} to Sarah, and she answers {{وَأَنْتَ؟}} “and you?”.

**Asking.** The question word comes first: {{مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟|min ayna anta?}} “Where are you from?”, word for word “from where you?”. And {{وَأَنْتِ؟|wa-anti?}} “and you?” turns any question back to the other person.

ex.note: said by a woman: the ending {{ة}} makes words feminine (a later lesson)
a question just by raising your voice

blocks.tip: The small marks above and below the letters are the vowels (a, i, u): the next lesson shows how to read them. Until then, the reading in Latin letters tells you how to say each example, and tapping an example lets you hear it.

mistakes.why: There is no “am” in the present: put {{أَنَا}} and the word side by side.
Sarah is a woman, so “you” is {{أَنْتِ}}, anti.

practice.q: You're talking to a woman. “You” is…
practice.why: {{أَنْتِ}}, anti, is for a woman; {{أَنْتَ}}, anta, for a man.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: {{أَيْنَ}} is “where”: min ayna anta?

practice.q: You're Sami, from Jordan. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: {{أَنَا}}. (Jordan is “the Jordan” in Arabic: {{الْأُرْدُنُّ}}.)

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Ask a man: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا…}}

answers.t: مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا جُون. أَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِيكَا.
answers.r: marḥaban, anā jūn. anā min amrīkā.
answers.tr: Hello, I'm John. I'm from America.

answers.t: أَهْلًا، أَنَا مَارِيَا. أَنَا مِنْ إِسْبَانِيَا.
answers.r: ahlan, anā māriyā. anā min isbāniyā.
answers.tr: Hi, I'm Maria. I'm from Spain.

lessons.title: Read any word in this course
lessons.summary: Learn the small marks that show the vowels, so you can read every example by yourself.
lessons.topic: The vowel marks: fatḥa, kasra, ḍamma, sukūn, shadda, and the doubled endings

goal.note: by the end of the lesson, you can read this without the Latin letters

blocks.p: Arabic is written from right to left, and most letters join the letter after them. The letters mostly write **consonants**; the short vowels a, i and u are small marks above or below the letters.

blocks.means: a sound like a, i or u, made with the mouth open. The other sounds of speech, like b, k or s, are **consonants**.

blocks.p: Newspapers and street signs usually leave the marks out: readers know the words. Every example in this course has them, because they show exactly how a word is said, and some of them, as you'll see, are grammar.

**Long vowels** are written with letters: {{ا}} for ā, {{و}} for ū and {{ي}} for ī, as in {{بَابٌ|bābun}} “a door”, {{نُورٌ|nūrun}} “light” and {{كَبِيرٌ|kabīrun}} “big”. In the readings, a line over a vowel (ā, ī, ū) means it is long: hold it about twice as long.

**Doubled marks at the end** of a word ({{ـٌ}}, {{ـً}}, {{ـٍ}}) add an n: {{كِتَابٌ|kitābun}}, {{كِتَابًا|kitāban}}, {{كِتَابٍ|kitābin}}. They mean “a”, as in “a book”. Which one a word has depends on its job in the sentence; later lessons explain. That's the -an at the end of {{شُكْرًا}} and {{جَزِيلًا}}.

Two more signs: {{ء}} (hamza) is a short catch in the throat, like the break in “uh-oh”; it often sits on an alif, as in {{أَنَا|anā}} “I”. {{ة}}, a round t, ends many words (the lesson on masculine and feminine explains it). In the readings, ʾ is a hamza, ʿ is the letter {{ع}} (a sound made deep in the throat), and a dot under a letter (ḥ, ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ) marks a heavier sound than the plain one.

blocks.tip: Read the Arabic first, then check with the reading under it. Tap any example to hear it.

mistakes.why: The n of -un is never written as a letter: the doubled mark ({{ـٌ}}) already says it.
“Big” has a long ī, written with {{ي}}: kabīrun. Short and long vowels make different words, so hold the long ones.

practice.q: Which mark is the vowel i?
practice.why: The kasra, a small line **below** the letter, is i.

practice.q: What does the doubled mark at the end of {{كِتَابٌ}} add?
practice.why: {{ـٌ}} is said -un, and it means “a”: kitābun, a book.

practice.q: Which word has a long ā?
practice.why: The {{ا}} after the first letter makes a long ā: bābun.

practice.q: Read the words, then put them in order.
Read this word aloud, then check: {{مُدَرِّسٌ}}
practice.why: The shadda on {{ر}} says it twice: mu-dar-ri-sun.

practice.q: Your turn: read these aloud without looking at the Latin letters, then write how you would thank someone: {{شُكْرًا جَزِيلًا}}, {{مَرْحَبًا}}, {{أَنَا مِنْ هُنَا}}

lessons.title: Say what you want
lessons.summary: Ask for things, and say what you want to do: “I want to learn Arabic.”
lessons.topic: {{أُرِيدُ}} and what you want; {{أَنْ}} and the -a form of a verb (the subjunctive)

dialog.t: لَا، شُكْرًا. وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أَدْفَعَ الْآنَ.
dialog.r: lā, shukran. wa-urīdu an adfaʿa l-āna.
dialog.tr: No, thanks. And I'd like to pay now.

blocks.p: **Wanting a thing.** {{أُرِيدُ|urīdu}} “I want”, then what you want: {{أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً.}} “I want a coffee.” The thing you want ends in -an here ({{قَهْوَةً|qahwatan}}, {{مَاءً|māʾan}} “water”, {{شَايًا|shāyan}} “tea”); a later lesson explains that ending, so for now just copy it.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: write, go, learn, want.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** Put {{أَنْ|an}} “to” between {{أُرِيدُ}} and the second verb. Compare:

table: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتَعَلَّمَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ.|urīdu an ataʿallama l-ʿarabiyyata.}}

blocks.p: Two things change. {{أَنْ}} comes in, and the verb's last vowel turns from -u into -a: {{أَتَعَلَّمُ}} becomes {{أَنْ أَتَعَلَّمَ}}. And both verbs say who: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ}} is, word for word, “I want that I go”.

blocks.means: a form of a verb used after certain little words, such as {{أَنْ}} “to”. In Arabic, the verb then ends in -a instead of -u.

ex.tr: I'd like a room for one night.
What do you want to eat?

blocks.tip: {{أُرِيدُ}} is polite enough in a shop or a café. Add {{مِنْ فَضْلِكَ|min faḍlika}} “please” (to a woman: {{مِنْ فَضْلِكِ|min faḍliki}}).

mistakes.why: Two verbs need {{أَنْ}} between them, and the second one ends in -a.
After {{أَنْ}}, the verb ends in -a, not -u.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: Two verbs: {{أَنْ}} between them.

practice.q: Which one means “I want to understand”?
practice.why: {{أَنْ}}, and the verb after it ends in -a.

practice.q: At the café: choose your replies.

lines.why: {{أُرِيدُ}} and what you want. ({{أَنَا شَايٌ}} would be “I am tea”!)

practice.q: Put the words in order.
How do you say “I want to learn Arabic”?
Your turn: what do you want to learn, and where do you want to go this year? Answer with {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ…}}

answers.tr: I want to go to Morocco.

answers.t: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتَكَلَّمَ مَعَ أَصْدِقَائِي بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ.
answers.r: urīdu an atakallama maʿa aṣdiqāʾī bi-l-ʿarabiyyati.
answers.tr: I want to talk to my friends in Arabic.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?” and answer “This is a book”: and see why some words are “he” and others “she”.
lessons.topic: {{هَذَا}} and {{هَذِهِ}} “this (is)”; masculine and feminine, and the ending {{ة}}

blocks.p: {{هَذَا|hādhā}} is “this”, and, as in the first lesson, “is” isn't said: {{هَذَا قَلَمٌ}} is “this (is) a pen”. {{مَا|mā}} asks “what?”: {{مَا هَذَا؟}} “What's this?”
But the mother says {{هَذِهِ|hādhihi}} for the watch. That's because every Arabic noun is either masculine or feminine, and the word for “this” changes with it.

blocks.means: a word for a person, an animal, a place, a thing or an idea: teacher, cat, Cairo, book, love.
whether a word is **masculine** (like “he”) or **feminine** (like “she”). In Arabic every noun has one, even the words for things: a pen is masculine, a watch is feminine.

blocks.p: **The sign of the feminine**: most feminine nouns end in {{ة}}, a round t called tāʾ marbūṭa. It sounds -a at the end of a sentence and -at- before an ending: {{سَاعَةٌ|sāʿatun}} “a watch”. Many words for people make their feminine by adding it:

A few common feminine nouns have no {{ة}}; learn them as you meet them: {{أُمٌّ|ummun}} “mother”, {{بِنْتٌ|bintun}} “girl”, {{شَمْسٌ|shamsun}} “sun”, {{يَدٌ|yadun}} “hand”, and the names of most countries and cities.

ex.tr: This is a student, and this is a teacher.

blocks.tip: The long ā in {{هَذَا}} (hādhā) and {{هَذِهِ}} (hādhihi) isn't written as a letter, but it is said all the same.

mistakes.why: {{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine (it ends in {{ة}}), so “this” is {{هَذِهِ}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: {{سَيَّارَةٌ}} ends in {{ة}}: feminine, so {{هَذِهِ}}.

practice.q: Which word is feminine?
practice.why: {{مَدِينَةٌ}} “city” ends in {{ة}}.

practice.q: {{أُمٌّ}} “mother” is…
practice.why: It has no {{ة}}, but a mother is a woman: one of the feminine words to learn by heart.

practice.q: A friend points at things in your bag. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{حَقِيبَةٌ}} “bag” is feminine: {{هَذِهِ}}. (And the word for “small” takes {{ة}} too: the next lessons show why.)

practice.q: A woman says “I'm a student”. What does she say?
Your turn: point at three things around you and name them with {{هَذَا…}} or {{هَذِهِ…}}.

lessons.title: Talk about “the” thing, not just “a” thing
lessons.summary: Say “a key” and “the key”, and ask where things are.
lessons.topic: {{الْـ}} “the”; the doubled mark means “a”; sun and moon letters

blocks.p: Arabic's word for “the” is {{الْـ|al-}}. It is written joined to the front of the noun: {{مِفْتَاحٌ|miftāḥun}} is “a key”, {{الْمِفْتَاحُ|al-miftāḥu}} is “the key”.

There is no separate word for “a”: the doubled mark at the end (-un) already means it. With {{الْـ}}, the doubled mark goes and a single mark is left. So it's {{الْمِفْتَاحُ}}, never {{الْمِفْتَاحٌ}}: a word can't be “a” and “the” at once.

**Sun letters.** Before 14 of the letters, the l of {{الْـ}} isn't said: the next letter is doubled instead (it gets a shadda), though the l is still written. {{الشَّمْسُ}} “the sun” is said ash-shamsu. These are called sun letters, after {{شَمْسٌ}} “sun”; the others are moon letters, after {{قَمَرٌ}} “moon”, and with them the l is said: {{الْقَمَرُ|al-qamaru}}.

table: Sun letters: the l is not said
Moon letters: the l is said
{{ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن}}
{{ء ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي}}

blocks.p: **After a vowel**, the a of {{الْـ}} isn't said either: {{أَيْنَ الْمِفْتَاحُ؟}} is ayna l-miftāḥu, and {{وَالْهَاتِفُ}} is wa-l-hātifu. The readings write it the way you hear it.

blocks.tip: Arabic also uses {{الْـ}} for things in general, where English uses nothing: “coffee is delicious” is {{الْقَهْوَةُ لَذِيذَةٌ}}, “the coffee is delicious”.

mistakes.why: A word with {{الْـ}} never has the doubled mark: that mark means “a”.
Before a sun letter the l is silent and has no mark of its own: say ash-shamsu.

practice.q: Choose the word that means “the car”.
practice.why: {{الْـ}} in front, and a single mark at the end.

practice.q: In which word is the l of {{الْـ}} **not** said?
practice.why: {{ش}} is a sun letter: ash-shamsu.

practice.q: {{مِفْتَاحٌ}} means…
practice.why: The doubled mark -un means “a”.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Point at a book and say “This is a book.”
Your turn: ask where three things or places are, with {{أَيْنَ…؟}}

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say “a big house”, “the old city”, and “The food is delicious”.
lessons.topic: Adjectives: after the noun, matching it in gender, “a/the” and ending

goal.tr: The old city is very beautiful.

dialog.tr: The hotel is lovely, and the room is big.

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, new, happy.

blocks.p: **Describing in a sentence**: as with “this is”, just put the two side by side: {{الْفُنْدُقُ جَمِيلٌ.}} “The hotel is lovely.” The noun has {{الْـ}}; the adjective hasn't. With a feminine noun, the adjective takes {{ة}} too: {{الْغُرْفَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ.}} “The room is big.”

**Describing inside a phrase** (“a big house”, “the old city”): the adjective comes **after** the noun and matches it in three ways: gender, “a” or “the”, and its ending. So “the old city” has {{الْـ}} twice: {{الْمَدِينَةُ الْقَدِيمَةُ|al-madīnatu l-qadīmatu}}.

That one {{الْـ}} makes all the difference: {{الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ}} is only a phrase, “the big house”; {{الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ}} is a sentence, “The house is big.” You can put both together: {{الْمَدِينَةُ الْقَدِيمَةُ جَمِيلَةٌ.}} “The old city is beautiful.”

mistakes.why: The adjective comes after the noun.
{{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine, so the adjective takes {{ة}} too.
With {{الْـ}} on both words it's a phrase, “the big house”. For a sentence, the adjective has no {{الْـ}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: Feminine ({{ة}}), and no {{الْـ}}: it's what you say about the car.

practice.q: “The new car” (a phrase) is…
practice.why: “The” on both words, and {{ة}} on both.

practice.q: {{الْمَطْعَمُ جَدِيدٌ.}} means…
practice.why: {{الْـ}} on the noun only: a sentence.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
How do you say “a beautiful city”?
Your turn: describe the place where you are now in two short sentences.

answers.tr: The room is small and nice.
The city is big and the weather is hot.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes-or-no questions, and ask who, what, where, when, how and how much.
lessons.topic: {{هَلْ}} for yes-or-no questions; question words first

goal.t: عَفْوًا، أَيْنَ الْمَحَطَّةُ؟ هَلْ هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ؟
goal.r: ʿafwan, ayna l-maḥaṭṭatu? hal hiya baʿīdatun?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the station? Is it far?

blocks.p: **Yes or no**: put {{هَلْ|hal}} in front of a sentence, and nothing else changes: {{هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ.}} “It's far.” → {{هَلْ هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ؟}} “Is it far?” In speech you can also just raise your voice at the end. The answers are {{نَعَمْ|naʿam}} “yes” and {{لَا|lā}} “no”.
Arabic's question mark faces the other way: {{؟}}. Before {{الْـ}}, {{هَلْ}} takes an i to join on: {{هَلِ الْمَطْعَمُ مَفْتُوحٌ؟|hali l-maṭʿamu maftūḥun?}} “Is the restaurant open?”
**Question words** come first, and the rest stays as it was: {{أَيْنَ}} + {{الْمَحَطَّةُ}} = “Where's the station?”

table: {{مَاذَا تُرِيدُ؟|mādhā turīdu?}} What do you want?
{{بِكَمْ هَذَا؟|bikam hādhā?}} How much is this?
{{لِمَاذَا أَنْتَ هُنَا؟|limādhā anta hunā?}} Why are you here?

ex.note: to a woman: ḥāluki; to a man: ḥāluka

blocks.tip: {{عَفْوًا|ʿafwan}} “excuse me” (it also means “you're welcome”) is the polite way to start a question to a stranger.

mistakes.why: {{هَلْ}} is only for yes-or-no questions; a question with a question word doesn't need it.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: {{أَيْنَ}}, ayna, is “where”.

practice.q: How do you ask “Is the hotel near?”
practice.why: Yes or no: {{هَلْ}} in front of the sentence.

practice.q: In a shop. Choose your replies.

lines.why: A yes-or-no question: {{هَلْ}} and the sentence.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Ask a woman where she's from.
Your turn: write three questions you'd ask someone you've just met.

lessons.title: Talk about other people: he, she, we, they
lessons.summary: Say who people are and what they do: “He's an engineer, and she's a doctor.”

goal.tr: He's an engineer, and she's a doctor.

dialog.tr: This is my brother. He's a student.
This is my sister. She's a teacher.
And where are you all from?

blocks.p: You know {{أَنَا}}, {{أَنْتَ}} and {{أَنْتِ}}. Here are all the words for people, the **pronouns**:

table: a man, or a masculine thing
a woman, or a feminine thing
any group with me in it
a group (of men, or men and women)

blocks.p: “It” is {{هُوَ}} or {{هِيَ}}, by the noun's gender: the station is feminine, so in the last lesson you asked {{هَلْ هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ؟}} “Is it far?”
{{أَخِي|akhī}} “my brother” and {{أُخْتِي|ukhtī}} “my sister” end in -ī, “my”: a later lesson shows how it works with every noun.

Arabic also has words for a group of women only ({{هُنَّ|hunna}} “they”, {{أَنْتُنَّ|antunna}} “you”) and for exactly two people ({{هُمَا|humā}}, {{أَنْتُمَا|antumā}}). You'll hear them less; a later lesson comes back to the two.

blocks.tip: Plurals for people often end in -ūna ({{مَشْغُولُونَ}} “busy”), but many change shape ({{أَصْدِقَاءُ}} “friends”). A later lesson explains; for now learn them as you meet them.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: {{هِيَ}}, hiya, is “she”.

practice.q: {{نَحْنُ}} means…
practice.why: {{نَحْنُ}}, naḥnu, is “we”.

practice.q: “The car? It's new.” Which word is “it”: {{السَّيَّارَةُ؟ ___ جَدِيدَةٌ.}}
practice.why: {{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine, so “it” is {{هِيَ}}.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
Introduce your friend Karim: “This is Karim. He's an engineer.”
Your turn: tell someone about two people you know: who they are and what they do.

answers.tr: This is my friend. He's a teacher.
This is my sister. She's a student.
